title: US Ends Duration of Status for Student Visas, Capping Stays at Four Years
excerpt: The DHS rule, effective September 15, replaces decades-old flexibility with fixed admission periods that universities warn will deter international students and drain the STEM pipeline.
body:
• DHS finalized a rule on July 17 ending "duration of status" for F-1 student and J-1 exchange visitor visas, replacing open-ended stays with a four-year cap effective September 15, 2026.
  • Students who need more time — including 97% of PhD candidates — must apply to USCIS for a formal extension or leave the country and re-enter, with no guarantee of approval.
  • Economists estimate the rule could cost the US economy $72–145 billion over a decade, with Indian students among the hardest hit as the largest group of international enrollees.

The Department of Homeland Security has finalized a sweeping rule that ends the decades-old "duration of status" system for international students, replacing it with fixed admission periods capped at four years. The regulation, published in the Federal Register on July 17, takes effect on September 15 and applies to roughly 1.2 million F-1 student visa holders and hundreds of thousands of J-1 exchange visitors currently in the United States.

Under the previous system, international students were admitted for as long as it took to complete their academic programs — a practice known as "duration of status" or D/S that had been in place since 1978. Under the new framework, U.S. Customs and Border Protection will issue a specific end date on each student's I-94 form, capped at four years regardless of program length.

What Changes for Students

Students whose programs exceed four years — which includes the vast majority of doctoral candidates — will now need to file a formal extension of stay application with U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, according to an analysis by the American Institute of Physics. The extension is not guaranteed and comes with a filing fee exceeding $400, with an additional $2,000 premium processing fee for those who need faster decisions.

The rule also shortens the post-completion departure grace period from 60 days to 30 days. Graduate students will be prohibited from changing programs or switching majors altogether. Students who complete a degree will not be allowed to pursue another at the same or lower level — meaning a PhD holder could not obtain a second doctorate or any lower-level degree on an F-1 visa.

After March 2027, students transitioning into Optional Practical Training will also need to file a separate USCIS extension, a step that was not previously required. OPT allows graduates to work in their field of study for one to three years and has been a critical pipeline for STEM workers entering the US workforce.

Economic and Academic Fallout

Universities and research organizations have pushed back sharply. More than 20,000 public comments were submitted during the rulemaking process, according to Brookings Institution researchers who analyzed the rule's impact. A study commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine estimated that the regulation could cause annual economic losses of $72 to $145 billion over ten years — more than 22 times the $3.3 billion cost that DHS itself projects.

"For decades, foreign students have been admitted into the US indefinitely, allowing thousands to abuse our immigration system by perpetually enrolling in courses to avoid having to leave."

— Markwayne Mullin, DHS Secretary

A survey of roughly 1,000 current international PhD students and postdoctoral fellows found that about half said they would not have come to the United States had the rule been in effect, according to the Brookings analysis. The Association of American Medical Colleges warned that the four-year cap makes it impossible for many physicians to complete critical residency and fellowship programs, potentially worsening a projected shortage of over 141,000 physicians by 2038.

Impact on Indian Students

Indian nationals represent the largest group of international students in the United States and are disproportionately concentrated in STEM graduate programs — the exact category most affected by the four-year cap. Indians also make up the largest share of OPT participants, using the program as a bridge to H-1B employment. With the new rule adding USCIS filing requirements to OPT transitions and giving the agency discretion to deny practical training, the pathway from student visa to work authorization becomes significantly more uncertain.

USCIS Director Joseph Edlow has publicly stated he plans to significantly limit post-graduation work opportunities for international students in all but "certain situations," according to the Brookings analysis — a stance that could effectively curtail the OPT pipeline that hundreds of thousands of Indian graduates rely on each year.

Legal and Political Outlook

DHS attempted a similar policy change during Trump's first term in 2018, but a court issued a preliminary injunction blocking it. The agency then published a proposed rule in September 2020, which was withdrawn by the Biden administration. This time, DHS went through the full notice-and-comment rulemaking process, though critics argue the agency did not adequately address the thousands of detailed objections submitted.

A bipartisan group of four congressional representatives has urged DHS to delay implementation, and 16 state attorneys general submitted comments opposing the rule. Legal challenges are widely expected once the regulation takes effect on September 15. Students currently in the US with D/S will be allowed to remain until their program end date, but no later than November 14, 2030.
